Math.title: Equal groups connect multiplication and division
Math.subject: Math
Math.instructions: Study the two examples before you work. Think: how many groups are there, and how many are in each group?
Math.explanation: Multiplication can find a total from equal groups. Division can split a total into equal groups or find how many groups fit. If 6 × 6 = 36, then 36 ÷ 4 asks how many groups of 4 make 36. The fact family helps us see that 9 × 4 = 36, so 36 ÷ 4 = 9.

workedExamples.title: Six bags with six cookies each
steps: Put 4 brownies in each new bag: 36 ÷ 4.
Nine groups of 4 make 36, so 36 ÷ 4 = 9 bags.

workedExamples.title: Share 24 counters into groups of 3
steps: Ask how many groups of 3 fit in 24.
Count by threes: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 — that is 8 groups.

visuals.alt: Nine boxes each contain four brownie dots, showing that 36 divided by 4 equals 9.
visuals.caption: Equal groups make the division visible.

English.title: Find the main idea and the details
English.subject: English
English.instructions: Read the original informational passage. Use its details to answer the questions.
English.passage: A wave can travel across the ocean while the water mostly moves up and down in place. A floating leaf rises and falls as a wave passes, but it does not usually travel all the way across the sea with that wave. Wind transfers energy to the water and helps create many ocean waves. When waves reach shallow water near a beach, they can change shape and break. Waves can move sand along a shore, so beaches may change over time. Studying waves helps people understand how energy moves and why coastlines are not always the same.

visuals.alt: A main idea box connects to three details from the text.
visuals.caption: The main idea should fit several details, not just one sentence.

English.scopeNote: This is original nonfiction practice for reading central idea and evidence. The guide lists ocean-themed books as possibilities, not a confirmed current classroom text.

Science.title: Follow water through the water cycle
Science.subject: Science
Science.instructions: Read the explanation and follow the arrows in the model. Then answer the questions and draw your own labeled model.
Science.passage: Water moves among Earth’s surface, the air, living things, and the ground. Sunlight can warm liquid water so some changes into water vapor and rises; this is evaporation. Water vapor cools and forms tiny droplets in clouds; this is condensation. Water can return to the surface as rain or snow; this is precipitation. It may flow over land as runoff or soak into the ground. Plants also release water vapor. The cycle has many paths, so it is better understood as a system than as one simple circle.

visuals.alt: A water-cycle model labels evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration, runoff, and infiltration.
visuals.caption: Follow the arrows; water can take many routes through the system.

Science.modelTask: On paper, draw a cloud, land, surface water, and a plant. Add arrows and label evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and either runoff or infiltration.

Social Studies.title: Why does geography matter?
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.instructions: Read the passage and examine the Earth image. Answer from the passage rather than guessing about a place from one picture.
Social Studies.passage: Geographers ask where a place is, what its land and water are like, and how people interact with the environment. A place can be described with both physical features, such as rivers and mountains, and human features, such as roads, buildings, languages, and work. Geography does not determine exactly how every person lives. It helps us ask useful questions and compare places carefully. The NASA image shows much of the Western Hemisphere, including North and South America. A single image can help with location, but it cannot tell us everything about the people who live there.

visuals.alt: NASA composite image of Earth’s Western Hemisphere, showing North and South America and surrounding oceans.
visuals.caption: A satellite composite can help orient a reader to continents and oceans; it is not a detailed political map.
visuals.credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center/Reto Stöckli, public domain via Wikimedia Commons.
